1:
The name of the country is unsettled in the manuscripts, and the witnesses divide three ways. Ellicott reports that the better copies give Gerasenes and some Gergesenes; Clarke finds Griesbach preferring Gerasenes and adds that the Gadarene territory lay within the Gergasene. Pseudo-Chrysostom argues for Gergesenes on geography, since Gadara is a city of Judaea with no sea about it at all and Geraza a city of Arabia with neither lake nor sea near it, so that the other readings would convict the Evangelists of a manifest falsehood about parts they knew well. Bede, who gives Geraza as a noted town of Arabia across the Jordan near mount Galaad, not far from the lake of Tiberias, evidently feels no such difficulty. Robertson settles it topographically rather than textually, finding the ruins of the village Khersa the likely site, within the district of Gadara some six miles off and nothing to do with the city of Gerasa thirty miles away. Lightfoot dissolves the quarrel by making the regions unequal, the Gergesene being of wider extent and containing the Gadarene within it, and derives the name either from the old Gergashite family of the Canaanites or, as he prefers, from the muddy soil the Jews called Gergishta.

Whether there was one demoniac or two is the older problem, and Augustine offers two answers without choosing. Either one of them was a more illustrious person, whose state much afflicted that country, or else Mark and Luke relate what was most worthy of compassion and therefore set down at greater length what had happened to this one; and he insists there is no discrepancy, since they never said there was one alone, which would have contradicted the other account. Henry reasons the same way in fewer words, that if there were two there was one, and Mark does not say there was but one. Wesley supposes this was the most remarkably fierce and ungovernable of them, and Robertson that one was perhaps more violent than the other, noting that each Gospel uses a different phrase for the condition. Clarke reports a sharper solution from Lightfoot, that one of the two was of Gadara and so a heathen while the other was a Gergesenian and so a Jew, and that Mark and Luke record the Gadarene because his was a singular case, the only heathen our Lord cured except the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman.
3:
The tombs are read for what they were and for what they were for. Gill notes that dwelling among them is one of the marks of a madman in Jewish reckoning, and adds that being in a heathen country would itself have made the man unclean had he not been possessed already. Henry explains the choice by the geography, that tombs lay outside the cities in desolate places, which gave the devil great advantage, since woe to him that is alone, and that the touch of a grave was polluting. Both he and Augustine then suspect a motive in it: Augustine says the devils dwelt in tombs wishing to convey the false opinion that the souls of the dead were changed into devils, and Henry adds the further advantage to them, that the mischief done might be laid to those souls rather than to themselves.

The broken bonds draw comment from every quarter. Ellicott argues from the two verbs that the fastenings need not have been metal at all, since snapping one by a convulsive movement and wearing the other away by friction rather suggests ropes or cords, as in the case of Samson. Robertson allows cords or even wooden stocks, notes that one word means rubbed or crushed together, and suggests the neighbours who told the story could point to the broken fragments. Clarke will have nothing but the supernatural, insisting the strength was beyond nature and turning aside to answer those who say there was no devil and the cases were only diseases, asking whom we should credit, the men sent from God or them. Calvin takes a middle course and states it carefully: madmen often show greater strength than their natural capacity allows, and we are not at liberty to deny that the devil does his part in such cases when God permits, but the force here described was far greater; and the shocking spectacle should remind us that bodily agony, however cruel, is not more to be dreaded than distress of mind. Henry turns the fetters into a figure, that the commands and curses of the law are chains upon sinners which some break in sunder like the wild ass; and on the gashing he offers a quieter guess than the others, that the cutting with stones may have been only his feet cut by the sharp stones he ran barefoot upon.
6:
The approach itself is staged carefully by those who notice it. Gill explains the apparent conflict with the other account by distance, since the tombs lay some way from the shore, so that the man came forth on sighting the landing and only recognised who it was on coming nearer, at which the power of Christ over the devils drove him forward sore against their wills. Robertson quotes the guess that he came at first perhaps with hostile intentions, and that the onrush of the naked yelling maniac must have tried the newly recovered confidence of the Twelve, whose surprise when he threw himself on his knees may be imagined. Ellicott specifies the posture exactly, not merely kneeling but touching the ground with the forehead in token of suppliant reverence. Barnes reads the act as an acknowledgement of Christ's power and of his control over fallen spirits, and Clarke as homage compelled by the power of God, asking how humiliating it must have been to Satan.

Calvin will not let the order of events pass unexamined, and his arrangement is the entry's one piece of narrative reconstruction. Christ first gave the command; only then did they pray and entreat; the complaint did not precede his words, and they did not complain that he tormented them until he urged them to go out. From this he draws the larger point, that they did not come of their own accord into Christ's presence but were drawn by a secret exercise of his authority, so that those who had been accustomed to carry men off in furious violence are themselves compelled to appear reluctantly at the tribunal of their judge; the whole of Satan's kingdom is thus under the government of Christ, and the rebellious complaints prove that the confession was not made from choice but drawn out by force. Ellicott reads the same sequence from the tense instead, taking the imperfect to mean that the demoniac interrupted our Lord while the words were still being uttered. Robertson reads the same tense as repetition, that Jesus had already ordered the demon out more than once before the outcry came.
7:
The title the demoniac uses draws a long note from Ellicott, who makes it the first occurrence of the name in the New Testament and takes the occasion to trace it. It belonged to the earliest stage of the patriarchal worship of one supreme Deity, since Melchizedek appears as its priest; it is used by Balaam as the prophet of a wider Semitic monotheism and by Moses in his great psalm; and in the Prophets and Psalms it tends to appear where there is some point of contact with nations that acknowledged one supreme God without being of the stock of Abraham. The Hebrew word found a ready equivalent in a Greek one that Pindar had already used as a divine name, which passed into the Greek Old Testament and became frequent among Greek-speaking Jews, occurring forty times in Ecclesiasticus alone. Being thus common ground between Gentile and Jew, it seems to have been used in formulas of exorcism — which, he suggests, is why it comes here from the lips of a demoniac, as the name of God most often sounded in his ears. He presses the point through the next verb too, from which our word exorcise derives, and notes that the man seeks in some sense to exorcise Christ, though in the language not of command but of entreaty. Robertson says the same more briefly, that the demoniac puts Jesus on oath.

What torment was feared is answered three ways. Bede offers two at once, that being cast out was itself considered a torment, or else that the spirit was invisibly tortured; and he explains the urgency by their calendar, since the devils knew a punishment awaited them at last and knew the time was not yet come, so that Christ appearing while they were doing such dreadful deeds made them fear the last times had been brought forward. He adds the plainer version: it is a great torment for a devil to cease to hurt a man, and the more severely he possesses him the more reluctantly he lets him go. Robertson locates the fear elsewhere, in the reluctance to return to the abyss just then, which was their real home and also the place of torment. Both he and Ellicott note that the verb properly means to test metals, and then to test a man by torture. Cyril describes the resulting manner rather than the motive, a devil divided between two passions, fear and audacity, hanging back and praying as if meditating a question, while the words of Christ are to him fire and flame.
9:
Why the question was asked at all is settled the same way by voices that rarely agree. Gill says it was not for Christ's own sake, since he was ignorant neither of the name nor of the number, but partly that the misery of the man's condition might be known and partly that the pity and power of his deliverer might be the more manifest. Theophylact says the Lord asked not because he required to know but that the rest might know there was a multitude dwelling in him, and adds a second reason of his own, that by fighting with us the devils make us more expert. Ellicott notices the narrative effect, that our Lord had spoken as though a single demon were in question and it is the man's own answer that discloses the name.

What the name means divides the arithmetical from the rhetorical. Robertson supplies the figure, that a full Roman legion had six thousand eight hundred and twenty-six men, observes that this may not have been a full one since the herd is numbered at about two thousand, and adds drily that a stickler for words might say each hog had several demons. Calvin denies that any number is intended, holding that the word denotes merely a great multitude, and Pseudo-Chrysostom says the same, that no fixed number is given because such accuracy would not help us to understand it. Lightfoot brings three kinds of evidence to the word: that among the Jews a legion was a common way of naming a great number, as in the saying that it is easier to nourish a legion of olives in Galilee than to bring up one child in the land of Israel; that among the Talmudists a legion bespeaks an unclean company, no legion being without some relic used in enchantments; and that the Romans themselves boasted of ten legions which could pull down heaven itself, from which he asks what the power of more than twelve legions of angels must be. Wesley reads the grammar instead and concludes that all were under one commander, who speaks throughout both for them and for himself.
10:
Calvin then turns the verse against a popular doctrine. There must have been good reasons why this man endured so severe a punishment as to have an army of devils dwelling within him, and what compassion it was to rescue one who had been more than a thousand times ruined; from which he infers how wretched a creature man is when deprived of the divine protection, since every man is exposed not to a single devil but may become the retreat of vast numbers. On that ground he rejects the common error, borrowed by Jews and Christians alike from the heathens, that each man is attacked by his own particular devil: Scripture rather declares that as it pleases God one devil is sometimes sent against a whole nation and many devils permitted against one man, as one angel may guard a nation and every man have many angels as his guardians. Clarke uses the same verse for a different argument, asking whether a disease could have spoken so, and settling the point from the parallel Gospel, where the inspired writer himself gives the reason for the name.

The request not to be sent away is read three ways. Clarke supposes the district mattered to them, since as a heathen region they might consider themselves in their own territories and act there with less restraint than where the worship of God was established. Calvin rejects the reading that has them merely avoiding uninhabited places and refers the plea to their appetite for mischief, since devils prowl among men like lions in search of prey and are grieved at being plunged into a deep where they will have no opportunity of ruining anyone. Ellicott reads the sentence psychologically, as a man half-conscious of his own being and half-identifying himself with the forces tormenting him, and so led to regard the great Healer as his tormentor. Gill draws the conclusion the scene invites, that the spirits which could not be held by chains are themselves held in chains, and cannot move an inch except as Christ is pleased to lengthen the chain; and Pseudo-Chrysostom adds why the harsher sentence was withheld, that Christ might have consigned them to the outer darkness at once and allowed them to remain in this world, lest the absence of a tempter should deprive men of the crown of victory.
11:
The herd is placed before it is destroyed, and the small differences are tidied up first. Gill reports that the mountains meant are those of Galaad or the range about Tiberias, and that the copies differ between a plural and a singular, several versions reading about the mountain or at the mountain. Augustine settles the corresponding difference between the Gospels without strain, since the herd was so large that some part of it stood on the mountain and the rest around it. Ellicott notes that the number two thousand is peculiar to Mark and counts it another instance of his graphic accuracy, while Clarke records that the word all before devils is missing from many copies and that Griesbach leaves it out. Gill keeps the force of the plural anyway, that the whole legion entreated and not merely their chief, all of them humble supplicants from fear and not love, and with a view to mischief.

Why the request was granted is the passage's difficulty, and the fathers answer it where Robertson refuses to. Bede says simply that he gave them leave so that by the killing of the swine the salvation of men might be furthered. Pseudo-Chrysostom makes it a demonstration, that Christ wished to show publicly the fury devils entertain against men and how much worse they would inflict if Divine power did not hinder them, and that since compassion would not allow this to be shown upon men it was permitted upon the swine. Remigius adds why swine and not something else: they did not ask to be sent into men because they saw that he whose power tortured them bore a human form, nor into flocks, since those are clean animals offered in the temple, but into swine, because no animal is more unclean and devils always delight in filthiness; and the asking itself proves that they cannot hurt anyone without divine permission. Robertson calls the words the crucial difficulty for interpreters and leaves it open, granting that it was better for hogs to perish than men but noting that the loss of property raises a difficulty of its own, akin to the problem of tornadoes and earthquakes. He does close off one exit: the suggestion that the man was merely exaggerating in the way a distressed person says he feels possessed by a thousand devils he dismisses as too easy an explanation. Theophylact reads the whole scene as a figure, since devils enter into men who live like swine, rolling in the slough of pleasure, and drive them down the precipice of perdition.

The aftermath is reported in small observed details. Robertson finds the imperfect tense picturing the disappearance of pig after pig in the sea. Gill has the keepers rather than the owners flee, astonished at the power of Christ, frightened by the noise of the devils and terrified at the loss. Bede supplies their motive, that they fled lest they perish with the herd, and then draws the consequence: the necessity of their loss brought these men to the Saviour, since God frequently confers a benefit on men's souls by making them suffer loss in their possessions. Lightfoot stops on the phrase about the country and shows from rabbinic usage that dwellers in the fields means the inhabitants of villages, private men in houses scattered here and there rather than built together as in towns; Robertson notes that Mark adds this to the city, so that the tale was carried both ways at once. Clarke records a further variant, that the better copies read they fed them rather than they fed the swine, a reading Griesbach adopts.
15:
What the townspeople saw is described as evidence before it is described as a shock. Barnes says there could be no doubt of the reality of the miracle, since the man had long been well known and an object of terror, and to see him all at once peaceful, calm and rational was proof that only the power of God had done it. Robertson notes the three participles, sitting and clothed and in his right mind, and the ingressive aorist that has them become afraid, adding that they had all been afraid of the man until now. Bede gives the same contrast from the other side, a man whom not even chains could bind now at the feet of him from whom he had obtained health, clothed where he had been continually naked. The clause that names his old condition is itself disputed: Ellicott treats it as a special form of antithesis between the man's past and present state given by Mark only, while Clarke reports that it is missing from several copies and that Mill, Bengel and Griesbach all think it should be dropped.

The fear is given four different contents. Barnes insists it does not mean they feared any evil would happen to them but that they were affected with awe, as in the presence of God. Calvin agrees so far and says they did right in it, since the majesty of God shone brightly in Christ, but makes their next act the worst thing they could have done, choosing to be deprived of the salvation offered them rather than endure his presence any longer; and he generalises, that though all wicked men adore God, they would if they had their choice withdraw to the greatest possible distance, since his face is terrible so long as they contemplate him as a Judge and not as a Father, which is why the gospel is so widely thought dismal and severe. Theophylact locates the fear in self-interest, that being saddened at the loss of their swine they feared suffering the like again. Bede offers a gentler reading altogether, that conscious of their own frailty they judged themselves unworthy of the presence of the Lord.

Whether the loss of the herd was the real motive is where the entry divides. Calvin argues it was not, on the ground of manner: if they had been exasperated by their losses they would not have besought him but would rudely have driven him out, whereas they honour him as God's minister even while dreading him. Wesley says almost the reverse in a line, that it is not improbable they might otherwise have offered some rudeness, if not violence. Robertson has no doubt where the motive lay, since pagan influence was strong in that district and the owners cared more for the loss of their property than for the healing of the wild demoniac, business coming first in the clash with spiritual welfare as it often does still. Theophylact puts the two together without ranking them, the loss and the fear of more loss. Gill notes only who it was that came, the inhabitants of the city and of the villages round about, and how earnestly they importuned him.
18:
The one refused request in the chapter is explained five ways. Gill gives three reasons at once: Christ was as able to preserve him absent as present, taking him along would have looked like the ostentation he was averse to, and he had work for the man to do in those parts. Barnes canvasses the conjectures and picks one, that Christ might have wished to leave him among the people as conclusive evidence, or to show the cure was complete and proof against the devils returning, but that the probable reason is simply that he desired to restore him to his family, being unwilling to prolong their anxiety. Clarke gives that reason alone, that he would not have the happiness of the man's relatives deferred. Theophylact adds the assurance behind the refusal, that though Christ himself was not present his power would keep him, and the purpose, that he might be of use in the healing of others. Gregory and Bede both read the refusal as an ordering of the Christian life: Gregory observes that when we have perceived ever so little of the divine knowledge we are at once unwilling to return to human affairs and seek the quiet of contemplation, whereas the Lord commands that the mind first toil hard at its work and afterwards refresh itself; Bede says the man who wished to remain signifies everyone who, after the remission of his sins, must work for a good conscience and serve the Gospel for the salvation of others before he rests in Christ.

Why this man was sent out to speak when others were silenced is answered by the geography. Chrysostom notices the inconsistency and resolves it in one sentence, that although Christ bade others whom he healed tell no one, he fitly bids this one proclaim it, since all that region, being possessed by devils, remained without God. Wesley says the same shortly, that it was peculiarly needful there, where Christ did not go in person. Robertson makes the contrast explicit, that in Galilee the healed were forbidden to tell because of undue excitement and misunderstanding, while here there was no danger of too much enthusiasm for Christ; and he observes that no people needed the message more than those who were begging Jesus to leave, so that the man was given the hardest task of all, to go home and witness there. He also corrects the rendering, that the phrase means his own folk rather than his friends.

The word Lord in the commission is read two ways with one result. Ellicott argues from the parallel Gospel, where the equivalent is God, that coming from our Lord's own lips the word must be taken in its Old Testament sense, referring not to the Lord Jesus but to the Father. Theophylact reaches the same place devotionally rather than philologically, marking the humility of the Saviour, who said not proclaim all things which I have done to you but all that the Lord hath done, and turning it into a rule, that when we have done any good thing we should take it not to ourselves but refer it to God. Barnes reads the man's obedience as the natural expression of right feeling and the model for anyone freed from sin. Gill supplies the place, very likely Gadara, where the man may have been a native and which he notes on ancient authority was reckoned within the Decapolis. Robertson follows the imperfect tense, that men kept on marvelling all over that district, and remarks that the man had a greater opportunity for Christ in his own home land than anywhere else.
21:
The crossing back is given a moral before the new scene starts. Henry observes that Christ did not stay to trouble the Gadarenes long, and turns it into a rule, that a despised gospel will cross the water and go where it will have better entertainment, since if some reject him others receive him. Augustine is more interested in the interval: the transition itself shows that the narrative follows the order of time, and there must have been some space here, since otherwise there would be no room for the feast the other Gospel relates. Gill fixes the geography, the crossing being that part of the lake needed to come from the country of Gadara back toward Capernaum.

The petitioner is identified with some care. Henry notes that he is unnamed in the parallel and named here, and explains the office two ways, either presiding in the synagogue worship or sitting as one of the judges of the consistory court which was in every city and consisted of twenty-three; and he marks the manner, that a ruler should address Christ with such humility and importunity, falling at his feet as one who knew he could obtain the mercy nowhere else. Wesley describes the institution behind the title, that every synagogue had a council of grave men with a president over them who was termed the ruler, and that sometimes there was no more than one ruler in a synagogue. Pseudo-Chrysostom explains why Mark gives the name at all, that it was recorded on account of the Jews of that time, so that the name might mark the miracle.

How ill the child was when the father spoke is the one point where the accounts visibly diverge, and three answers are offered. Pseudo-Chrysostom harmonises by compression: the other Gospel has the ruler report that she was dead where Mark has her very sick with the news of her death arriving later, but the fact is the same, and it was for brevity that she is described as already dead. Augustine explains it differently, that the other evangelist attaches himself not to the words of the father but to what was most important, his wishes, since he was in such despair that his wish was for her to return to life, not thinking she could be found alive at all. Henry offers the plainest account, that he said one thing at first and another upon fresh information sent to him. Robertson simply sets the three states side by side without reconciling them, at the point of death in Mark, just dead in Matthew, and dying in Luke, calling it a tragic moment for Jairus.

The small words draw the closest attention. Robertson finds the diminutive an endearing touch peculiar to Mark and notes that the words for I pray thee are not in the Greek; Clarke renders it that little daughter of mine and says the phrase expresses much tenderness, adding from the parallel that she was an only daughter of about twelve. Lightfoot supplies the legal sense of the word from rabbinic usage, that a daughter is called little until she is twelve years old complete, and from twelve years and one day is called a young woman. Ellicott renders it literally, that she is at the last point. Whether the father's faith was equal to the occasion is less agreed. Theophylact thinks him faithful only in part, since falling at the feet of Jesus was well done but begging him to come was not, and he ought rather to have said, speak the word only. Gill reads the response as the answer to that, that Jesus went with him immediately and without objecting to the weakness of his faith. Robertson watches the crowd, pressing so close with a verb found nowhere else in the New Testament except a few verses later, that Jesus could hardly move or even breathe.
25:
Before the cure is described the case is documented, and two witnesses do it at length from the same rabbinic source. Lightfoot and Clarke both set out the prescriptions a Jewish physician would have tried on such a patient: gum of Alexandria, alum and crocus, each by weight, bruised together and given in wine; failing that, Persian onions boiled in wine, with the command to arise from the flux; failing that, the woman set where two ways meet holding a cup of wine while someone comes behind and frightens her; failing that, a handful each of cummin, crocus and fenugreek boiled in wine; and, as Clarke adds, seven trenches dug and vine cuttings burnt in them while she is led from one to the next. From some of these, Clarke concludes, it is evident she could not be bettered and from others that she must have been made worse, so that with the expense and the years it is perfectly credible she spent all she had, and she was therefore a fit patient for the Great Physician. Robertson draws the opposite moral from the same list: the doctors were not to blame, since she had a disease they did not know how to cure, and he adds that the physician among the evangelists neatly takes care of the physicians by saying only that she could not be healed of any.

Who she was is reported and then doubted. Gill relays from Eusebius the tradition that she belonged to Caesarea Philippi, where her house was still shown, with a brass figure of a kneeling woman with outstretched arms and, facing it, a figure of a man in a tunic with his hand stretched toward her, at whose feet a strange plant grew up to the hem of the brazen robe and was a remedy against all diseases; the monument is said to have stood until his own day, and Theophylact reports that it was broken to pieces under Julian the apostate. Gill himself thinks it more likely she was an inhabitant of Capernaum, in whose streets the crowd was pressing. Ellicott notes that the detail about growing worse is absent from the parallel and is, as usual, more graphically expressed here.
27:
Why she approached from behind is given three explanations that do not compete so much as layer. Chrysostom answers from the Law, that she was unclean by it, and that being celebrated and known to all she did not dare to come in front but only ventured on the hem; and he adds the correction the whole story needs, that it was not the hem of the garment but her frame of mind that made her whole. Barnes reads the same movement as an act of faith mixed with conscious unworthiness, illustrating how a sinner comes to God for pardon, full of confidence in the power and trembling at the approach. Robertson puts it simply as timidity bred by the disease and an unwillingness to attract attention. Clarke admires the execution rather than the motive, that she formed her resolution in faith and carried it out with courage notwithstanding her weakness, and finds it now crowned with success.

The moment of cure is described from her side rather than his. Gill shows that the phrase about the fountain of her blood is ordinary Jewish idiom, both for the source of such an issue and for its drying up, the womb being commonly so called and a woman pronounced pure only when the fountain was dry. Ellicott calls the clause about her feeling it in her body another graphic and characteristic touch, giving not only the fact but the woman's consciousness of the fact, and Robertson reads the verb as knowledge and the moment as a vivid one of joy. He also glosses the word for her affliction, which properly means a whip used in flagellations and came to be used of sufferings regarded as a scourge from God. Theophylact and Bede then read the woman as a figure, Theophylact making her human nature, which sin had made to spill its blood and which the wise men of this world and of the Law and the Prophets could not cure, healed the moment it touched his flesh; Bede making her the Church gathered from the nations, which came behind because it did not see the Lord present in the flesh and yet attained the grace of his faith.
30:
What went out of him is defined before it is explained. Ellicott takes the word in its old medical sense, the power or force that brings about a definite result, as men once spoke of the soporific virtue of a drug, and says it is used here with like technical precision of the supernatural power that flowed out at the touch of faith. Barnes glosses it simply as power to heal. Pseudo-Chrysostom guards it against the obvious misunderstanding: the virtues of Christ do not go out of him locally or corporally, nor pass away from him in any respect, but being incorporeal they go forth to others and are given to others without being separated from their source, as a teacher gives sciences to his pupils. Gill insists on the will behind it, that the cure came not without his knowledge and not without his will, and entirely by his power.

Whether the healing was a conscious act is the question Robertson raises and refuses to close. He notes that scholars argue both ways, some holding that Jesus healed by conscious will and others that it was an unconscious response to her appeal, and some even that the healing followed his becoming aware of her reaching for help; what we do know, he concludes, is that Jesus was conscious of the going out of power from himself. He compares the two Gospels on the verb, one having simple knowledge and Mark a fuller and clearer perception, and adds an observation that outruns the case, that no real good can be done without the outgoing of power, which is true of mother, preacher, teacher and doctor alike. He is equally plain that there was no magic in the garments, allowing that there may have been superstition in the woman's mind but holding that Jesus honoured her darkened faith as he did in the matter of Peter's shadow and Paul's handkerchief.

Why the question was asked when the answer was known is settled by three witnesses to the same effect. Barnes says it was not to obtain information, since he had healed her and must have known on whom the blessing fell, but that she might herself make confession of the whole matter, by which the power of her faith and the greatness of the miracle might be manifested. Bede gives the purpose more sharply, that she should confess the truth of her long want of faith and of her sudden belief and healing, so being confirmed herself and affording an example to others. Pseudo-Chrysostom adds the negative reason, lest the virtue of the miraculous work should be consigned to oblivion.

The disciples' objection produces the entry's finest distinction. Robertson reports their amazement at his sensitiveness to the touch of a crowd, and says they little understood the drain on him from all this healing, which pulled at his heart-strings and exhausted his nervous energy. Pseudo-Chrysostom answers the objection directly: the crowds who throng him cannot be said to touch him, since they do not come near him in thought and in faith. Clarke says the same as a warning, that many touch Jesus who are not healed by him, because they do not do it by faith through a sense of their want and a conviction of his willingness. Bede turns the contrast ecclesiological, one believing woman touching the Lord while the crowd merely presses. Ellicott and Robertson both stop on the tense of the looking, which implies a continued scrutiny; and Robertson quotes the summary the whole scene turns on, that Jesus knew the difference between touch and touch.
33:
Why she was afraid is answered more fully here than anywhere else in the chapter. Gill offers four possibilities without choosing among them: that she should be reproved and suffer the penalties of the law for appearing in public while unclean; that Christ was displeased at the method she had taken; that he might recall the cure; or that he was angry at her attempt to slip away undiscovered and without thanks. Theophylact gives a shorter reason and a memorable phrase for it, that she feared because she had stolen her health. Robertson keeps to what the narrative shows, that she had heard the question and felt his gaze, so that secrecy was no longer possible, and reads the participles as a portrait of a woman who had tried to hide in the crowd and now had to come and confess. Ellicott notes only that the whole description is fuller than in the parallel.

The address that answers her fear is examined word by word. Gill marks the contrast first, that instead of reproving her he called her daughter, which was an affable and courteous form of speech among the Jews but may signify more here, a spiritual relation, since she was a daughter of Abraham by natural descent and also one who walked in the steps of his faith. Bede grounds the title in the cure itself, that he calls her daughter because she was saved by her faith, for faith in Christ makes us his children. Barnes reads it as a word of kindness meant to inspire confidence and dissipate her fears. Theophylact explains why the declaration was made publicly at all, and gives three reasons: to approve her faith, to urge the ruler of the synagogue to a confident hope that his child could be cured the same way, and to free the woman herself from fear.

The two clauses of the blessing are each read closely. On the first, Bede insists on the tense, that he said not thy faith is about to make thee whole but has made thee whole, so that in believing she had already been healed. On the second, Barnes and Clarke agree against the obvious rendering, that the words mean continue whole rather than be whole, since she was cured already, and Clarke adds that it therefore carries a promise, that the disorder should afflict her no more. Ellicott turns to the farewell and concedes the idiom is too settled to change while noting that the Greek properly means go into peace; Robertson suggests the word carries more of the Hebrew sense of health of body and soul. Theophylact reads it as rest after long pain and torture, and Pseudo-Chrysostom as a sending away into the final good, since God dwells in peace, so that she was healed not only in body but from the causes of bodily pain, that is, from her sins. Calvin draws the conclusion that makes the words necessary rather than decorative: the benefit she had obtained was fully ratified only when she heard from the lips of Christ what she had already learned from experience, since we do not truly or with a safe conscience enjoy God's benefits in any other way than by possessing them as contained in the treasury of his promises.
35:
The messengers assume the case is closed, and the witnesses agree about why. Clarke says these people seem to have had no other notion of our Lord than that of an eminent physician, who might be useful while there was life but afterwards could do nothing. Barnes says the same from the other side, that they had as yet no confidence he could raise the dead and supposed his power over her ended with her life. Theophylact makes the assumption explicit, that those about the ruler took Christ for one of the prophets and thought he should be asked to come and pray over the girl, but that once she had expired there was no point in asking. Robertson notes that he had already raised the widow's son at Nain but that people in general did not expect him to raise the dead, and traces the verb in the messengers' question, which in the older poets means to skin or flay and comes to mean to vex or annoy; Ellicott gives the same primary sense and corrects the title, which is strictly the Teacher. Robertson adds that the news arrived opportunely for the woman just healed, since it drew attention away from her.

Whether the answer is a rebuke is the entry's real question. Augustine says firmly that it is not. The narrative never says the ruler assented to the friends who wished to spare the Master the journey, so be not afraid, only believe is not a reproof for want of faith but was intended to strengthen the belief he already had; and Augustine adds why it matters, that if he had joined them in saying Jesus should not be troubled, the words the other Gospel puts in his mouth would contradict what was in his mind. Clarke reads the timing as pastoral, the words spoken the instant the news arrived so as to forestall the distress the father must otherwise have felt. Calvin takes it as a warning that fear and distrust might shut out a grace to which death is no hindrance, and enlarges it into a rule: God would be far more liberal in his communications to us if we were not so narrow, and we cannot go beyond bounds in believing, since our faith however large will never embrace the hundredth part of the divine goodness. Robertson finds a further possibility in the verb, which ordinarily means not heeding but may here carry the sense of overhearing something not addressed to him; either way, he says, Jesus ignored the conclusion the messengers had drawn.

Why only three disciples were admitted is answered four ways. Chrysostom says it was to take away all display while still leaving witnesses of his divine power, the three chief disciples with the father and mother being needed above all. Theophylact makes the same point of the whole scene, that Christ in his lowliness would do nothing for show. Gill has him dismiss the multitude as one not desirous of the honour and applause of men, and guesses that what he said to the ruler was spoken privately and in a low voice. Calvin offers two reasons and does not choose, that they were unworthy witnesses or that he would not have the miracle overpowered by a noisy crowd, and adds what he thought better, that the young woman whose dead body they had seen should suddenly come out before their eyes alive and full of vigour. Robertson supplies the least exalted explanation, that the house was probably too small; and he notes that this is the first appearance of the inner circle of three, seen again at the Transfiguration and in Gethsemane. Wesley accounts for the odd way the third is named, that when Mark wrote, not long after the ascension, the memory of James lately beheaded was so fresh that his name was better known than his brother's.
38:
The noise in the house is described precisely, and the descriptions carry a judgement. Barnes calls it confusion and weeping, the wailing being inarticulate mournful sounds, a howling for the dead. Ellicott identifies the verb as the one used elsewhere of the clanging of a cymbal, formed from an interjection and applied to inarticulate cries of despair or of victory alike. Robertson calls it an onomatopoetic word going back to Pindar, notes that soldiers entering battle raised the same cry, and applies it here to the monotonous wail of hired mourners; he adds that Jesus, having just dismissed one crowd, found the house occupied by professionals making bedlam as though ostentatious noise were evidence of grief. Gill fills in the personnel, the pipers and the mourning women singing their doleful ditties, and notes at the next verse that these were people who got their livelihood that way.

The saying that she sleeps is taken by every witness as true and by none as a denial of death. Pseudo-Jerome states the resolution in one line, that both reports are true, since the meaning is, she is dead to you but to me she is asleep. Bede expands the same thought and traces a usage from it: to men she was dead, who were unable to raise her up, but to God she was asleep, in whose purpose the soul was living and the flesh resting to rise again, whence it became a custom among Christians that the dead, who will certainly rise, should be said to sleep. Calvin agrees that sleep everywhere in Scripture denotes death and that the comparison drawn from temporal rest points to a future resurrection, but insists that Christ here makes an express distinction in order to excite an expectation of life, meaning that they would presently see raised the girl they supposed dead. Robertson puts it in the plainest modern terms, that Jesus undoubtedly meant she was not dead to stay dead, and notes that some have taken him to mean the child was never dead at all.

The laughter is then turned against the mockers. Theophylact says they laughed as at one unable to do anything further, and that in doing so he convicts them of bearing witness involuntarily that she was really dead whom he raised, so that their scorn establishes the miracle. Calvin makes the same argument and adds that we should not be surprised at being laughed at by thoughtless and ignorant people wholly engrossed in profane lamentation, since this very circumstance was an additional confirmation, those present entertaining no doubt whatever as to her death. Bede draws the consequence for the narrative, that because they chose rather to laugh than to believe they are deservedly excluded from the room as unworthy to witness the power and the mystery of her rising. Ellicott and Robertson both note the tense, which has them keep it up; Robertson calls the loud laughter ill suited to the solemn occasion, observes that Jesus had to use pressure to make the hired mourners go, and remarks that the presence of some people will ruin the atmosphere for spiritual work. Clarke explains who was kept in rather than who was put out, since prudence required the parents to be present as witnesses, and notes that our Lord gave this preference to the same three disciples on three important occasions, the Transfiguration, this raising, and the agony in the garden; he adds that the participle describing the girl as lying is textually very doubtful and is dropped by Griesbach.
41:
The Aramaic words are preserved, and the first question is why more is translated than was said. Jerome states the charge and answers it: someone may accuse the Evangelist of a falsehood in his explanation, since the two words mean only damsel, arise, and the added clause is his own; but it was added to express that his meaning was to call and to command her. Lightfoot answers the same charge differently and more finely. The words themselves sounded no more than maid, arise, but in the pronouncing of them such authority and commanding power shone forth that they sounded no less than if he had said, I command thee, arise. He sets it beside the physicians' formula already met in this chapter, where the practitioners told a woman to arise from her flux, meaning only that they wished she would; Christ says arise, and means that he commands it.

What the words themselves are is disputed in a smaller way. Barnes calls the phrase the language which our Saviour commonly spoke, a mixture of Syriac and Chaldee. Ellicott is more cautious and draws the opposite inference from the fact that these syllables were remembered: it would probably be too wide an inference to assume that our Lord ordinarily spoke Greek, but Greek was current throughout Palestine, and the stress laid on the Aramaic here, as in the Ephphatha and in the cry from the cross, shows that such words attracted a special notice. Robertson has Peter hearing and remembering them and Mark interpreting for those without the language, notes the diminutive that makes her a little girl, and quotes a broad dialect rendering of the command. Clarke records the oddest variant in the chapter, a reading in the Codex Bezae that turns the opening word into an address to a master, and judges one common spelling of the second word certainly faulty.

The manner of the raising is read for what it shows. Chrysostom notes that life is restored both by the hand and by word of mouth, the hand having a quickening power that quickens the dead body and the voice raising her as she lies; and he takes the walking as proof that he had raised her really and not only to the eye of fancy. Calvin says the words could naturally do nothing to recall the senses of a dead girl, and that Christ meant a magnificent display of the power of his voice, which reaches even to the dead and exerts a quickening influence on death itself, so that men might be accustomed to listen to his doctrine. The Gloss reads the age as an explanatory note, added to show she was old enough to walk, and takes the walking as proof that she was not only raised but perfectly cured. Ellicott draws a different conclusion from the same detail, that Mark gives the age at the end and Luke at the beginning while Matthew omits it altogether, which he counts a proof of real independence in the handling of the common material.
43: The two closing commands are read as a pair, and the first divides the witnesses. Gill and Wesley agree on the motives for silence, a dislike of ostentation and popular applause, the avoiding of further offence to the Scribes and Pharisees, and the prevention of any attempt to proclaim him king, the hour for his death and full manifestation not being come. Calvin doubts the fact could have stayed hidden at all and thinks it would have been improper to suppress such a display of the power of God; he suggests instead that the silence was about the manner rather than the fact, and only for a time, so that the parents might in quietness revolve the work of God — and he rejects as unnatural the solution of those who make the prohibition a device for whetting people's desire. Robertson doubts it more bluntly, asking whether they would keep still, and pointing out that there was the girl besides. On the second command all are agreed and only the emphasis differs. Barnes says he raised her by extraordinary power but willed that she should be sustained by ordinary means, and that the eating gave full evidence of a real restoration, as the risen Saviour afterwards ate with his disciples. Clarke draws the general rule from a heathen poet's advice, that miraculous power should be resorted to when it is necessary and ordinary means used when it is not, since to do otherwise would be to tempt God. Lightfoot finds a rabbinic parallel in which a healed man asks for food in the same hour, and reads the request as evidence not merely of life but of perfect health. Wesley states the principle for both kinds of life at once, that when either natural or spiritual life is restored, even by immediate miracle, all proper means are to be used to preserve it. Robertson quotes the summary the detail deserves, that she could walk and eat, and so was not only alive but well; and Ellicott draws a source-critical inference from it, that a detail given here and in Luke but absent from Matthew suggests the fuller report came from someone who had been present in the chamber where the miracle was wrought. Clarke, having begun with the poet, ends further out still, holding that those taught by Christ have their understandings improved as well as their souls saved, so that true religion, civilisation, mental improvement, common sense and orderly behaviour go hand in hand.
